title: Problem set 4: Mass transfer
summary: Practice with diffusion: the Cottrell equation, diffusion-layer growth, Ficks laws, transport numbers and the role of the supporting electrolyte.

intro.text: Chapter 4 supplies the transport relations used everywhere else: the Cottrell equation i = nFAD^(1/2)C/(pi^(1/2)t^(1/2)), the diffusion-layer thickness d = sqrt(pi D t), and Ficks laws of diffusion.
Remember the three modes of transport - diffusion, migration and convection - and that a supporting electrolyte removes migration so diffusion alone remains.

blocks.text: Chapter 4 supplies the transport relations used everywhere else: the Cottrell equation i = nFAD^(1/2)C/(pi^(1/2)t^(1/2)), the diffusion-layer thickness d = sqrt(pi D t), and Ficks laws of diffusion.
Remember the three modes of transport - diffusion, migration and convection - and that a supporting electrolyte removes migration so diffusion alone remains.

questions.question: Use the Cottrell equation i = nFAD^(1/2)C/(pi^(1/2) t^(1/2)) with n = 1, A = 1.0 cm2, D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s, C = 1.0e-6 mol/cm3 and t = 1.0 s. Calculate i in microamperes (F = 96485, pi = 3.1416).
The diffusion-layer thickness is roughly d = sqrt(pi D t). Calculate d in micrometres for D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s and t = 1.0 s.
Fick-1s first law gives the flux J = D(dC/dx). Calculate J in mol/(cm2 s) for D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s and a concentration gradient of 1.0e-3 mol/cm4.
In a solution the cation carries 60 percent of the current. What is the anion transport number t-?
questions.explanation: Transport numbers sum to one, so t- = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40.

questions.question: By what factor is the Cottrell current at t = 9 s smaller than at t = 1 s? (Answer as a fraction, e.g. 0.5.)
questions.explanation: The current falls as t^(-1/2), so the ratio is sqrt(1/9) = 1/3 = 0.333.

questions.question: How long, in seconds, does it take for the diffusion layer to reach d = 100 um (1.0e-2 cm) if D = 1.0e-5 cm2/s? Use t = d^2/(pi D).
An excess of supporting electrolyte is added to a solution mainly to:
options: Eliminate migration of the analyte and fix the ionic strength
questions.explanation: The supporting electrolyte carries the current by migration, so the analyte moves by diffusion alone; it also fixes ionic strength and reduces resistance.

questions.question: In an unstirred solution with excess supporting electrolyte, the analyte is transported to the electrode by diffusion alone.
questions.explanation: Migration is suppressed by the supporting electrolyte and convection is absent, so the transport of the analyte is purely diffusive.

questions.question: Which modes of transport can carry material to an electrode? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Diffusion, migration and convection are the three transport modes in solution. Nuclear decay is not a transport process.

questions.question: The Cottrell current decays in proportion to the square root of time.
questions.explanation: i is proportional to t^(-1/2), so it decays gradually as the diffusion layer thickens.

questions.question: Which equation describes how concentration changes with both position and time?
questions.explanation: Ficks second law is the continuity equation for diffusion, expressing how concentration evolves in space and time; the first law gives the flux from a gradient.

questions.question: The Cottrell current is proportional to t^(-1/2). If i = 172 uA at t = 1.0 s, what is i in uA at t = 0.25 s?
The Cottrell slope m = i t^(1/2) equals nFAD^(1/2)C/pi^(1/2). If i = 172 uA at t = 1.0 s, what is m in uA s^(1/2)?
Besides suppressing migration, a supporting electrolyte also:
options: Lowers the solution resistance and fixes the ionic strength
questions.explanation: The supporting electrolyte carries the current, reducing resistance, and buffers the ionic strength so activity coefficients stay constant.

questions.question: With a large excess of supporting electrolyte, the migration of the analyte is negligible.
questions.explanation: The abundant inert ions carry essentially all the migration current, so the dilute analyte moves by diffusion alone.

questions.question: Which variables appear in Ficks second law for one-dimensional diffusion? Select all that apply.
options: The second derivative of concentration with distance
The change of concentration with time
questions.explanation: Ficks second law involves D, the curvature of the concentration profile and the time derivative. Colour plays no part.
